assumptions.text: Ideas stays supporting, not core. Decision D1 took option C (orchestrator, D15): the subdomain is split by module. Plan validation is a domain-model module: it holds the rules of coverage, the DAG, judge pairing, the model guide and the declared gates. Idea intake and worker questions stay active-record. The judgment work (research, interview, assumptions, spec, plan) is done by the sub-orchestrator model, not by fleetd code. Scored diff 6, cplx 5.
Core stays the minority: 2 of 6 subdomains (task-execution, integration). Ideas would make 3 of 6, which is half, not a minority (ticket rule for this run).

The 2 cores use domain-model: state rows are the truth, and the events table is the audit trail that the one door writes beside each row in the same transaction (design, Ledger, rule 1 One door). Decision D2 took option A (orchestrator, D15): a domain model with an events table, not event-sourced.

Fleet runtime is supporting, not generic. Its pane hosting (herdr) and host services (launchd, systemd, Windows service) are adopted and only wrapped, as understand N14 says. The single ledger writer and the command channel have no product to buy, so the subdomain as a whole is built. The platform layer is the leaf crate crates/horch-platform (design A19). It is not part of fleet-runtime and has no subdomain (decompose N7).

Worktree custody is supporting with medium investment. Its no-loss rule (rescue ref written and read back before any removal) is 1 invariant over a 8-state lifecycle, not an algorithm; a failure breaks G2, so it gets invariant tests and fault-injection tests.

Worker profiles is supporting with medium investment because it owns the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY scrub (C2, an absolute operator rule). Its complexity is the rate of change of the agent CLIs, not domain rules.

Every subdomain has evolution custom: each has at least 1 custom capability. The commodity and product capabilities of fleet-runtime (host services, pane hosting) are adopted systems, not built parts.

decisions.question: Is the ideas subdomain core or supporting?

options.summary: Supporting, active-record: a flat idea state machine in code; the planning judgment stays in the sub-orchestrator model.
pros: The dispatcher is deterministic and small by design (design, Ideas: the dispatcher and sub-orchestrators)
Spends aggregate design on the stall and landing rules, where the failures of today are
cons: 24 events and 21 commands is a large state machine for active-record
Approval hash and 'no task outside a plan' are invariants a flat model can let slip
risks: Plan validation rules grow and the flat model leaks them into callers

options.summary: Core, domain-model: the idea and plan are aggregates with invariants (approval hash, 1 feature per idea, no task outside a validated plan).
pros: Protects the C5 rule (only the operator approves) inside 1 aggregate
cons: 3 of 6 subdomains core is not a minority
Much of the complexity is model work done by the sub-orchestrator, not fleetd code
risks: Core budget is split 3 ways for 1 team

options.summary: Split: plan validation is a supporting module with domain-model rules; idea intake and questions stay active-record.
pros: Puts rich rules only where the invariants are
cons: Decompose has 1 subdomain here; a split re-opens step 3
Adds a boundary nobody asked for
risks: Re-runs decompose for a small gain

decisions.rationale: Decided by the orchestrator (D15). The operator can reverse it. Chosen: C. Plan validation is a domain-model module (it holds the rules of coverage, the DAG, judge pairing, the model guide and the declared gates). Intake and questions stay active-record. Reason: these plan rules are real invariants, and they decide whether a task may start; a flat model lets them leak into callers. The split is a module boundary inside the ideas context, not a new subdomain, so decompose stays as it is. The step recommended A: Recommendation: A. The strongest argument against it is that plan validation and the approval hash are real invariants; ddd-code can still give the plan aggregate invariant tests inside a supporting context. The design does not settle the classification, so the operator decides.
would_flip_if: Plan validation rules turn out to need more than 1 aggregate
The operator names the idea pipeline as the reason to use fleetd
An idea bug, not a task stall, is the main failure in the first runs

decisions.question: Do the core subdomains use domain-model with an audit event table, or event-sourced-domain-model?

options.summary: domain-model: state rows are the truth; transition() writes the row and 1 event in 1 transaction; events are audit.
pros: Matches rule 1 One door literally (design, Ledger)
Reconciler reads rows each pass; no replay cost
Today's ledger is row-based (schema v7), so migration is smaller
cons: 'Derived tables' in the design can be read as projections
risks: Row and event can disagree if a bug writes one without the other

options.summary: event-sourced-domain-model: the events table is the truth and the task, attempt, branch and feature tables are rebuilt from it.
pros: Full history for forensic replay of a stall or a lost branch
Matches 'event log plus derived tables' read strictly
cons: Replay and projection rebuild add work to every schema migration
The reconciler is level-triggered on rows, not on events
risks: A failed migration that loses events loses state, not only history (05 L-4)

options.summary: Mixed: event-sourced for task and attempt only, domain-model for integration.
pros: History where the stall forensics need it

decisions.rationale: Decided by the orchestrator (D15). The operator can reverse it. Chosen: A, a domain model with an events table, not event-sourced. This is the recommendation of the step. Recommendation: A. The strongest argument against it is the design's own phrase 'derived tables'. The design does not settle which store is the truth, so the operator decides.
would_flip_if: The operator needs 'state as of' queries for a past pass
The design means the derived tables are rebuilt from events
Row and event drift is seen in fault-injection tests

classifications.rationale: core - G1 (no task stalls silently) and G4 (use the subscription usage fully) are won or lost here; today's alternative is the long-lived orchestrator conversation with claims and a lazy watchdog, whose stalls are the reason for fleetd; rule 2 (diff >= 7); cplx 8 from the earned lease, the stall ladder, fallback and waiting_quota with a paused lease, retries, replan and the verifier with review scripts and paired judges; nothing to buy.
classifications.evolution_rationale: custom: cap-task-supervision, cap-task-verification and cap-usage-pacing are all custom; no product leases agent attempts across CLIs and usage pools.
classifications.future_direction: Decisive core (both scores >= 8): the big investment, aggregates for task, attempt and verification with invariant tests for I1, I2 and I4. Review in 6 to 12 months; usage pacing can move to supporting once the pacing rule is stable (bet B3).

classifications.rationale: core - G3 (each idea reaches the primary branch through its feature) depends on it, and G2 on its no-loss branch invariants; today's alternatives are hand reconciliation of task branches and hosted merge queues, which work on pull requests to a protected base, not on local task branches, and find no conflicts between in-flight features; rule 2 (diff >= 7); cplx 8 from bundles behind the fast gate, bisection, trial merges, stacking with resolver tasks and continuous rebases.
classifications.evolution_rationale: custom: cap-feature-integration is custom. Merge queues are a product for pull requests, but not for local task branches with a ledger row per branch.
classifications.future_direction: Core, not decisive (diff 7). Feature and task-branch aggregates own the landing state machine and the no-loss rows 04 F5, F7, F9, F11, L5, L9. If a hosted merge queue later supports local branches, the bundle and bisect part can become supporting (table-stakes former core); trial merges and stacking stay core (bet B2).

classifications.rationale: supporting - G3 depends on it, and today's alternative is ideas typed into 1 orchestrator conversation; rule 3 (diff 6 with cplx 5 is below the core rule); cplx 5 because fleetd code runs 1 fixed idea state machine and the judgment work is done by the sub-orchestrator model (A1). Pattern domain-model for the plan validation module only (D1 option C, orchestrator D15): coverage, the DAG, judge pairing, the model guide and the declared gates are invariants. Intake and questions stay active-record. Medium investment: it feeds the core task-execution with committed plans.
classifications.evolution_rationale: custom: cap-idea-intake, cap-idea-planning and cap-operator-attention are custom.
classifications.future_direction: Hidden core: the hard part (research, interview, assumptions, plan) is done by the sub-orchestrator model. Keep the dispatcher, intake and questions flat (active-record). Give plan validation an aggregate with invariant tests, and keep the approval hash under test. Review in 6 to 12 months.

classifications.rationale: supporting - G2 (no work a worker paid for is lost) depends on it; today's alternative is worktrees made by workers and orphaned on disk; rule 3 (diff 6, cplx 5); cplx 5 from 1 lifecycle of 8 states and 1 invariant (rescue ref written and read back before any removal, design I6); git does the work and is wrapped. Medium investment because a failure breaks G2 (A5).
classifications.evolution_rationale: custom: cap-worktree-custody is custom; git worktrees are a commodity, the custody rules around them are not.
classifications.future_direction: Supporting, kept simple: a worktree row per lifecycle plus a reconciler against git worktree list. Fault-injection tests for rows 04 W6, W8, W9. No timeline to change.

classifications.rationale: supporting - G4 needs a fallback persona for every worker persona and G1 needs a liveness feed from each CLI; today's alternative is the teammates roster and agent CLIs run by hand; rule 3 (diff 5); cplx 4 from mapping 1 profile to the flags, environment and files of each CLI and from conformance tests. Medium investment because it owns the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY scrub (C2) and the CLIs change every week (C10).
classifications.evolution_rationale: custom: cap-agent-cli-adaption is custom; no product maps 1 profile to every agent CLI.
classifications.future_direction: Supporting, kept as 1 adapter per CLI behind 1 profile shape. If the agent CLIs converge on 1 headless protocol, adapters move to transaction-script glue.

classifications.rationale: supporting - G1 needs a daemon that is itself watched; today's alternative is horch ledger watch, the lazily started watchdog; rule 3 (diff 3 but not solved elsewhere as a whole, so rule 1 does not fire); cplx 4 from the single ledger writer, the command channel and the supervision of the daemon on 3 OSes (C3). Pane hosting (herdr) and host services (OS service managers) are adopted and wrapped, not built (understand N14, A4). The platform layer is a leaf crate outside every context (decompose N7). Medium investment: a hang stops the whole fleet.
classifications.evolution_rationale: custom: cap-fleet-record is custom; cap-host-services is commodity and cap-pane-hosting is product, and both are adopted as existing systems.
classifications.future_direction: Supporting, kept thin. The herdr adapter and the service manager calls are adapters, not models. D16 settled the old question of understand Q2: Phase P moves all 178 OS-specific sites into crates/horch-platform before Phase 1, so fleet-runtime calls the platform interface and owns no OS module.

bets.text: A deterministic daemon with earned leases replaces the LLM orchestrator, and no task stalls silently.
bets.risk: The lease misreads activity: a slow but healthy worker loses its lease, or a sleep and wake on 1 OS expires every lease (discover H13).
bets.validate_by: Phase 2 fault-injection tests (kill -STOP a worker; alarm within 1 lease) and 0 tasks left assigned with an expired lease (G1 metric).

bets.text: Parallel features with trial merges, stacking and resolver tasks reach the primary branch through 1 pull request each, with no hand reconciliation.
bets.risk: Resolver tasks grow past their size limit, or stacking chains features so 1 slow feature holds others.
bets.validate_by: The resolver size limit and structural merge tool tests (understand Q7) on the recorded conflicts of this repository.

bets.text: Pacing dispatch to each pool's usage window, with fallback personas, uses the subscription usage fully and burns no attempt on a usage limit.
bets.risk: No target for 'full use' exists (understand Q1), so the bet cannot fail visibly.
bets.validate_by: 0 attempts burned by a usage limit in Phase 2, and a target set for unused usage per window.

summary: 2 of 6 subdomains are core: task-execution (decisive) and integration. Ideas, worktree-custody, worker-profiles and fleet-runtime are supporting and built simply; only the plan validation module of ideas gets a domain model (D1 option C). The ledger is a domain model with an audit events table, not event-sourced (D2 option A). Nothing is generic: herdr and the OS service managers are adopted inside fleet-runtime as adapters. Every subdomain is built in horch-core, and the platform layer is the leaf crate crates/horch-platform.

notes_for_downstream.text: Sharpens understand N14 and follows decompose N7: fleet-runtime builds only the single ledger writer, the command channel and the herdr adapter. herdr and the OS service managers are adopted systems behind adapters; no context models panes or services. The platform layer (crates/horch-platform) is a leaf crate outside fleet-runtime.

Aggregates go to task-execution, integration and the plan validation module of ideas (domain-model, D1 option C). Plan validation holds coverage, the DAG, judge pairing, the model guide and the declared gates. Idea intake, questions, worktree-custody, worker-profiles and fleet-runtime are active-record with invariant tests (approval hash, rescue ref before removal, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY scrub).
The 1 decisive core (task-execution) fits the 1 team. The same team owns integration, the second core; no core needs a second team.

D2 option A (orchestrator, D15): the ledger is a domain model with an events table, not event-sourced. transition() writes the state row and 1 event in 1 transaction; the row is the truth, and no table is rebuilt from events.

plain_words.what: We decided which parts of fleetd need the most careful design, and which parts stay simple.
plain_words.decided: 2 of 6 parts are core: running and checking tasks, and landing branches on features. The other 4 parts are built simply, except the plan checks of the ideas part, which get a careful model. The ledger rows are the truth, and the events table is an audit log. We buy nothing new. herdr and the OS service managers are used as they are.
plain_words.assumed: The ideas part is not core, because an AI does its hard thinking and the code is 1 fixed state machine plus the plan checks.
plain_words.riskiest: If the simple parts of the ideas part (intake and questions) grow rules, the flat design there will leak bugs.
